prompt: Compare V filing year 2024 and V filing year 2025, with the exact SectionItem filter "Item 1A": retrieve the disclosed risks from regulation of interchange rates in each filing year. Retrieve evidence separately for each filing year.

hops.rationale: The passages fully support the original goal of identifying risks from regulation of interchange rates in V's 2024 Item 1A. Passage 000002 says changes to interchange fees, by mandate or otherwise, can substantially affect payments volume and net revenue. Passage 000003 covers the U.S. Federal Reserve debit interchange cap and proposed lower rates, proposed congressional credit-routing legislation, state laws restricting interchange assessment, and the EU IFR caps with possible further reductions. Passage 000004 covers Latin American interchange caps, Asia Pacific and other regulated markets, and government pressure to drive down MDR. Passage 000005 covers cross-border interchange regulation, the UK PSR review, and network-fee scrutiny. Passage 000000 frames interchange reimbursement rates as a regulatory difference across jurisdictions. Adjacent pairs 000002 through 000005 connect without gaps.

As a global payments technology company, we are subject to complex and evolving regulations that govern our operations. See Item 1—Government Regulation for more information on the most significant areas of regulation that affect our business. The impact of these regulations on us, our clients, and other third parties could limit our ability to enforce our payments system rules; require us to adopt new rules or change existing rules; affect our existing contractual arrangements; increase our compliance costs; and require us to make our technology or intellectual property available to third parties, including competitors, in an undesirable manner. Verified filing excerpts (extractive audit evidence; no derived calculations):

- Regulations adopted by the U.S. Federal Reserve cap the maximum U.S. debit interchange reimbursement rate received by large financial institutions at 21 cents plus 5 basis points per transaction, plus a possible fraud adjustment of 1 cent. [V-2024-10K-item1A-p000002](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1403161/000140316124000058/v-20240930.htm) (chunk: `000140316124000058#item1A#passage-000002`; accession: `0001403161-24-000058`).
- In Europe, the EU’s IFR places an effective cap on consumer credit and consumer debit interchange fees for both domestic and cross-border transactions within the EEA \(30 basis points and 20 basis points, respectively\). [V-2024-10K-item1A-p000003](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1403161/000140316124000058/v-20240930.htm) (chunk: `000140316124000058#item1A#passage-000003`; accession: `0001403161-24-000058`).
- The European Commission has announced its intention to conduct another impact assessment of the IFR, which could result in even lower caps on interchange rates and the expansion of regulation to other types of products, services and fees. [V-2024-10K-item1A-p000004](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1403161/000140316124000058/v-20240930.htm) (chunk: `000140316124000058#item1A#passage-000004`; accession: `0001403161-24-000058`).
- Cross-border MDR is also regulated in Costa Rica and Turkey. In June 2022, the UK’s PSR initiated a market review focusing on post-Brexit increases in interchange rates for transactions between the UK and Europe. [V-2024-10K-item1A-p000005](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1403161/000140316124000058/v-20240930.htm) (chunk: `000140316124000058#item1A#passage-000005`; accession: `0001403161-24-000058`).
- If the District Court of North Dakota’s decision is affirmed on appeal and ultimately prevails, it could potentially result in the Federal Reserve setting a significantly lower interchange cap for relevant debit transactions in the U.S. [V-2025-10K-item1A-p000003](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1403161/000140316125000089/v-20250930.htm) (chunk: `000140316125000089#item1A#passage-000003`; accession: `0001403161-25-000089`).
- While the Illinois law remains subject to legal challenge, if such laws are allowed to go into effect, they may also impose significant technical and compliance burdens on our business. [V-2025-10K-item1A-p000003](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1403161/000140316125000089/v-20250930.htm) (chunk: `000140316125000089#item1A#passage-000003`; accession: `0001403161-25-000089`).
- In Asia Pacific, the Reserve Bank of Australia \(RBA\) which already regulates interchange, recently proposed reducing existing interchange caps on domestic credit and debit transactions and not allowing differential interchange treatment for consumer and commercial transactions. [V-2025-10K-item1A-p000004](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1403161/000140316125000089/v-20250930.htm) (chunk: `000140316125000089#item1A#passage-000004`; accession: `0001403161-25-000089`).
- Most recently, in July 2025, New Zealand adopted interchange caps on cross-border transactions including commercial credit transactions. Australia has also proposed adopting caps for cross-border transactions. [V-2025-10K-item1A-p000005](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1403161/000140316125000089/v-20250930.htm) (chunk: `000140316125000089#item1A#passage-000005`; accession: `0001403161-25-000089`).
